body:
Architecture, Wine + Music: SHARE Friends’ Evening
MA Studio & Partners Hosts the Architecture Community in Tirana

Tirana · Architecture · Conversation · Wine · Music

Architecture is shaped not only at the drawing table, but also through encounters, conversations and the exchange of ideas.
In this spirit, MA Studio & Partners opens its studio in Tirana to host Architecture, Wine + Music: SHARE Friends’ Evening — an intimate gathering bringing together architects, designers, urban planners, landscape architects, collaborators and friends of the profession.

Created together with SHARE Architects, the evening offers a more informal setting for the architecture community to meet beyond conferences, presentations and project meetings.
A studio. A glass of wine. Music in the background. And a room filled with people who share a curiosity for architecture, cities, design and the ideas shaping our built environment.
When Architecture Becomes Conversation

Architecture is fundamentally collaborative.

Behind every building, interior, landscape or urban intervention lies a network of conversations between architects and engineers, designers and craftspeople, clients and consultants, institutions and communities.
SHARE Friends’ Evening brings that culture of exchange into a more personal environment.

Hosted inside MA Studio & Partners, the gathering transforms the architecture studio from a place of production into a place of encounter.
There are no formal boundaries between speaker and audience. Instead, the evening is conceived around conversation: discovering projects, exchanging perspectives, meeting new collaborators and reconnecting with familiar faces from the architecture and design community.

Wine and music become part of that atmosphere creating the space for discussions to develop naturally.

SHARE Architects: Connecting Architecture Across the Region
For more than 25 years, SHARE Architects has contributed to building one of the most active professional architecture networks across Central and Eastern Europe.

Through international forums, conferences, awards, professional meetings and cultural initiatives, SHARE has created connections between architects, designers, urban planners, landscape architects, contractors, academics and emerging professionals.

Its platforms have become an important source of continually updated information for the profession while supporting the continuous development of specialists and providing visibility to new generations of architectural talent.
But the strength of an architectural community is not built through major conferences alone.

It is also built through smaller encounters.
Through introductions.
Through conversations that continue after presentations end.
Through friendships and collaborations that begin unexpectedly.
SHARE Friends’ Evening in Tirana brings precisely this dimension of the network into focus.
MA Studio & Partners: Opening the Studio
Hosting the evening at MA Studio & Partners gives the gathering a particular character.

An architecture studio carries traces of ideas in progress: drawings, materials, models, references, unfinished questions and projects gradually taking shape.
Opening that environment to the wider professional community creates a different relationship between architecture and its audience.

For one evening, the studio becomes a shared space.

A place where established architects can meet emerging talent. Where designers can encounter people from other disciplines. Where local perspectives can connect with the wider regional network represented by SHARE Architects.
Rather than presenting architecture as a finished object, the evening celebrates the culture surrounding its creation.
Architecture + Wine + Music
The concept is intentionally simple.
Architecture provides the common language.
Wine invites people to stay, talk and discover one another.
Music creates the rhythm of the evening.
Together, they create an atmosphere somewhere between a studio visit, a salon and a gathering among friends.
Because some of the most valuable professional exchanges happen precisely when the formal program ends.
A conversation over a glass of wine can become a collaboration.
An introduction can become a future project.
A discussion about a city can develop into an idea.
And an evening among colleagues can gradually strengthen an entire creative community.
Tirana as a Meeting Point
There is particular relevance in bringing this format to Tirana.

The city is experiencing an extraordinary period of architectural and urban transformation. Albanian studios increasingly work alongside international practices, while a new generation of architects and designers is developing its own perspective on contemporary architecture, interiors, landscape and urban life.

This evolution makes Tirana not simply a location for architectural events, but an increasingly interesting meeting point within the wider European design conversation.
Creating spaces where this community can meet informally is therefore essential.

Architecture, Wine + Music: SHARE Friends’ Evening is one such space.
Not simply an event about architecture, but an evening for the people who create it.
A celebration of ideas, relationships and creative exchange.

And perhaps, between architecture, wine and music, the beginning of the next conversation worth continuing.
Architecture, Wine + Music
SHARE Friends’ Evening
Hosted by MA Studio & Partners
In collaboration with SHARE Architects
Tirana, Albania
Architecture brings us together.
Conversation moves us forward.

posts.title: Designing the Profile of the Future Architect
posts.excerpt:
Designing the Profile of the Future Architect
Ervin Taçi for SHARE Architects
As technology transforms the way we design, cities grow increasingly complex, and architecture gains access to unprecedented tools for creating new forms, architect Ervin Taçi returns to something fundamentally simple.
body:
Designing the Profile of the Future Architect
Ervin Taçi for SHARE Architects
What kind of architect does the future need?
As technology transforms the way we design, cities grow increasingly complex, and architecture gains access to unprecedented tools for creating new forms, architect Ervin Taçi returns to something fundamentally simple:
the human scale.
His contribution, “Designing the Profile of the Future Architect,” was included in the international editorial project and book developed by SHARE Architects — a collection bringing together thoughts, architectural manifestoes and interviews from 100 architects from around the world.
Rather than attempting to predict what the buildings of tomorrow will look like, Taçi addresses a more fundamental question:
Who should the architect of tomorrow become?
His answer begins not with technology, form or spectacle, but with people.
The Future Begins with the Human Scale
The challenges facing architects have changed dramatically over the last century.
Following the Second World War, economic expansion and industrialisation accelerated the growth of cities around the world. New housing models, infrastructure and large-scale urban development responded to an urgent need for expansion.
But something essential was often lost in the process.
The human dimension of the city.
Large buildings were separated by disproportionately large open spaces. Urban planning increasingly prioritised systems, vehicles and efficiency, while the pedestrian experience and the social role of public space were frequently pushed into the background.
For Taçi, understanding this history is essential when discussing the future of architecture.
Because the architect of tomorrow must also respond to the consequences of yesterday's planning decisions.
The challenge is no longer simply to expand cities.
It is to make them liveable.
Creating Cities for People
After decades in which the human dimension was often neglected, cities around the world are rediscovering the importance of pedestrian life and public space.
Walking, meeting, sitting, observing, playing and interacting may appear to be ordinary activities.
Yet collectively, they create urban life.
A successful city must therefore do more than accommodate buildings and infrastructure. It must create the conditions for people to encounter one another.
This means shorter walking distances.
Attractive public spaces.
A diversity of urban functions.
Safer pedestrian environments.
And neighbourhoods where everyday activities can coexist.
Urban planning becomes directly connected to social sustainability.
When people are invited to walk, remain in public space and interact with one another, architecture and urban design begin to strengthen the social fabric of the city.
The architect's responsibility therefore extends far beyond the limits of an individual building.
Architecture Is Not Only About Form
One of the strongest ideas in Ervin Taçi's contribution is his critique of architecture understood primarily as an exercise in form.
Contemporary architectural culture has often celebrated buildings for their ability to attract attention.
Iconic silhouettes.
Unexpected geometries.
Spectacular façades.
Architecture designed to become an image.
The global media environment has reinforced this tendency, creating a culture in which buildings can sometimes be evaluated according to their visual impact before their contribution to everyday urban life is considered.
But architecture cannot exist independently from the city surrounding it.
A building is part of an urban organism.
Regardless of whether it is spectacular or restrained, monumental or modest, every building influences its context.
It changes movement.
It creates boundaries.
It produces shadows.
It defines public and private space.
It influences how people experience the street.
Architecture must therefore be understood not simply as form, but as an interaction between form and life.
From Object to Relationship
This distinction fundamentally changes the role of the architect.
Instead of asking only:
What should this building look like?
The architect begins asking:
How will people approach it?
How does it meet the street?
What happens around it?
What kind of public space does it create?
How does it contribute to the neighbourhood?
What relationships can emerge between the building and the people who use it?
These questions shift architecture away from the isolated object and toward a network of relationships.
Architecture + People
Building + Public Space
Form + Life
City + Human Scale
The quality of architecture begins to depend not only on the object itself, but on what happens around and within it.
Tirana Olympic Park: Architecture and Urban Life
Within his contribution, Taçi refers to Tirana Olympic Park, developed by DEA Studio, as a representative example of the studio's approach to architecture and urban design.
The project demonstrates an interest in architecture that extends beyond the individual building toward the relationship between movement, public space, landscape and human activity.
Rather than seeing architecture as an autonomous object, the project considers how different elements can work together as part of a larger urban experience.
The architecture becomes activated by people.
Movement becomes part of the composition.
Public space becomes part of the project.
The relationship between buildings becomes as important as the buildings themselves.
This way of thinking represents a recurring principle in Taçi's approach:
architecture should participate in city life rather than simply occupy the city.
Borea Ski Resort: Architecture at the Scale of Territory
The contribution also references Borea Ski Resort, a complex project integrating urban design and architecture.
Here, the architectural question expands to an even larger scale.
The architect must consider not simply an individual object but an entire system: buildings, movement, landscape, infrastructure, public space and human experience.
Projects of this complexity reveal why the architect of the future cannot operate within the boundaries of a single discipline.
Architecture increasingly requires the ability to think across scales.
From detail to building.
From building to public space.
From public space to masterplan.
From masterplan to landscape.
The architect becomes a coordinator of relationships.
Technology Will Change. The Human Scale Must Remain.
The future architect will inevitably work with technologies radically different from those available to previous generations.
Digital design has already transformed architectural practice.
Parametric tools, computational design, advanced simulation, new materials, fabrication technologies and increasingly artificial intelligence are changing how architects analyse, visualise and produce architecture.
These technologies create extraordinary possibilities.
But they also introduce an important question:
What remains constant when the tools continuously change?
For Ervin Taçi, the answer is clear.
The human being.
Technology can optimise.
It can calculate.
It can generate.
It can simulate.
But the architect must continue asking what all of these capabilities ultimately serve.
Innovation should expand architecture's possibilities without allowing architecture to lose sight of its purpose.
Remember for Whom We Design
This becomes the central message of Ervin Taçi's contribution to Designing the Profile of the Future Architect.
As the profession adapts to continuous technological development and innovation, the architect must not lose the human scale as the focal point of design.
And ultimately, the architect must remember:
for whom are we designing?
It is a deceptively simple question.
Yet it can transform an entire project.
Because architecture is ultimately experienced by people.
Not from the masterplan.
Not from the rendering.
Not from the architectural photograph.
But from the ground.
At eye level.
While walking through a street.
Entering a building.
Sitting beneath a tree.
Crossing a public square.
Living inside a home.
The future of architecture may therefore depend not only on how advanced our tools become, but on how successfully we continue to understand the people those tools are meant to serve.
Part of a Global Architectural Conversation
Ervin Taçi's text forms part of “Designing the Profile of the Future Architect,” the first editorial project developed by the SHARE Society.
The publication brings together contributions from 100 architects from around the world, collected through SHARE International Architecture Forums across Central and Eastern Europe.
Thoughts, manifestoes and interviews were brought together around a shared question: how should the architectural profession evolve in response to the profound transformations affecting cities, society, technology and the environment?
The diversity of perspectives is precisely what gives the project its relevance.
There may be no single profile of the future architect.
But there are fundamental responsibilities that the profession cannot afford to forget.
The Architect of Tomorrow
The architect of the future will need to adapt.
To understand new technologies.
To work across disciplines.
To respond to environmental challenges.
To operate across different scales and increasingly complex urban systems.
But progress should not be measured only by the sophistication of our buildings or the technologies used to create them.
It should also be measured by the quality of the environments we create for people.
Cities that invite us to walk.
Public spaces that encourage us to meet.
Architecture that contributes to its surroundings.
Buildings that participate in life rather than simply becoming objects to be observed.
The tools will evolve.
The city will evolve.
The profession will evolve.
But one question should remain at the centre of architectural thinking:
For whom are we designing?
For Ervin Taçi, the answer defines the profile of the future architect:
Adapt to innovation. Embrace technology. Understand the city. But never forget the human scale.

posts.title: Open Lecture at Epoka University of Architect Ervin Taci: Designing the Context
posts.excerpt: Within the framework of ARCH 505 – Special Topics in Architectural Design, architect Ervin Taçi delivered an open lecture titled “Designing the Context” at EPOKA University, sharing with architecture students insights drawn from professional practice, international experience and the realities they will encounter beyond university.

source.label: Open Lecture at Epoka University of Architect Ervin Taci: Designing the Context

body:
Open Lecture at Epoka University of Architect Ervin Taci: Designing the Context
Designing the Context 
Ervin Taçi Open Lecture at EPOKA University

Architecture begins with context — but designing within context requires understanding far more than the physical conditions of a site.
Within the framework of ARCH 505 – Special Topics in Architectural Design, architect Ervin Taçi delivered an open lecture titled “Designing the Context” at EPOKA University, sharing with architecture students insights drawn from professional practice, international experience and the realities they will encounter beyond university.

The lecture created a bridge between architectural education and professional life, exploring one of the most fundamental questions in contemporary practice: How should architects respond when designing within different physical, social and cultural contexts?
From Architectural Education to Professional Practice
Architecture school teaches students how to observe, research, conceptualise and design.
Professional practice introduces another layer of complexity.

The architect must learn to negotiate between ideas and reality — between design ambition, the client, the site, regulations, budgets, construction methods and the cultural environment in which a project will ultimately exist.
A central aim of Ervin Taçi’s lecture was therefore to share fragments of professional life that students will encounter once they graduate.
Rather than presenting architecture exclusively through completed buildings and polished images, “Designing the Context” offered a perspective on the thinking, decisions and challenges behind the architectural process.
It is in this transition from concept to reality that the architect’s role becomes particularly complex.

What Does It Mean to Design the Context?
Every architectural project begins somewhere.
A site.
A city.
A landscape.
A climate.
A community.
But context is not simply the physical location surrounding a building.
It is also history, culture, behaviour, materials, climate, economic conditions and the ways in which people understand and inhabit space.
To design within context therefore requires more than responding to dimensions, orientation or topography.
It requires observation and interpretation.
The architect must first understand a place before attempting to transform it.
This idea formed the conceptual foundation of Taçi’s lecture.
Context should not be treated as a limitation to creativity. It can become the generator of architecture itself.
Designing Across Cultures
One of the central case studies presented during the lecture explored a project developed in Africa, offering students an opportunity to examine the challenges of designing outside the architect’s familiar cultural environment.
Working in another country inevitably changes the architectural process.
Assumptions that may appear natural within one cultural context can become irrelevant in another.
Climate changes.
Materials change.
Construction traditions change.
Social relationships with space change.
Even fundamental concepts such as privacy, community, circulation and the relationship between indoor and outdoor environments can carry different meanings.
The challenge for the architect is therefore not to arrive with a predetermined architectural language and impose it upon the site.
The challenge is to listen to the context first.
From Observation to Design Strategy
Designing in an unfamiliar environment requires curiosity.
Before drawing, there must be research.
Before form, there must be understanding.
Through the African project presented during the lecture, Taçi introduced students to innovative design strategies developed in response to a different cultural and environmental reality.
The project demonstrated how architecture can emerge through an interpretation of local conditions rather than through the repetition of familiar solutions.
Culture becomes design information.
Climate becomes design information.
Local patterns of living become design information.
Materials and construction knowledge become design information.
The architect’s task is to bring these elements together and transform them into a coherent spatial strategy.
In this sense, designing the context does not mean reproducing the context.
It means understanding its underlying logic and using that knowledge to create something contemporary, relevant and specific to its place.
Architecture Between the Local and the Global
The discussion also raises a wider question facing contemporary architecture.
Today, architects increasingly operate internationally.
Projects cross borders. Studios collaborate across countries. Images, technologies and architectural references circulate globally almost instantaneously.
Yet architecture ultimately remains physical.
Every building belongs somewhere.
This creates an important tension between global architectural knowledge and local identity.
An architect may bring international experience, technological knowledge and new design methodologies to a project, but these must ultimately enter into dialogue with the specific conditions of the place.
The objective is not necessarily to choose between global and local.
It is to discover how the two can inform one another.
The Albanian Context
The lecture also opened a conversation about professional practice closer to home.
Students had the opportunity to ask Ervin Taçi questions about his experience working within the Albanian architectural context, connecting the theoretical discussion to the realities of architecture in Albania.
For young architects preparing to enter the profession, this dialogue is particularly important.
The transition from university to practice introduces questions that cannot always be answered within the design studio alone.
How does an architect defend an idea?
How does the original concept survive the development process?
How do you respond to constraints without losing architectural quality?
How do you work with clients, engineers and other disciplines?
And how does an architect develop a personal position while continuously responding to changing contexts?
There are rarely universal answers.
Professional experience is built precisely through confronting these questions repeatedly.
Architecture as a Continuous Learning Process
One of the most valuable lessons behind “Designing the Context” is that architectural education does not end with graduation.
If anything, graduation marks the beginning of another form of education.
Every new project teaches the architect something.
A new site introduces different constraints.
A new client introduces another perspective.
A different country challenges established assumptions.
An unfamiliar culture requires new ways of observing.
Professional practice therefore becomes a continuous process of learning, questioning and adapting.
For an architect, experience should not eliminate curiosity.
It should deepen it.
Connecting Practice and the Next Generation
Open lectures such as this one create an important connection between professional practice and architectural education.
Students gain access not only to projects, but to the experiences behind them — including uncertainties, decisions, constraints and lessons that rarely appear in the final photographs of a building.
For practicing architects, these encounters are equally valuable.
The questions of students can challenge established assumptions and reopen conversations about the fundamentals of architecture.
In this way, architectural knowledge becomes something that is continuously exchanged rather than simply transferred from one generation to another.
Designing Begins with Understanding
The central message behind Ervin Taçi’s “Designing the Context” extends far beyond a single lecture or project.
Architecture does not begin with form.
It begins with observation.
With understanding the site.
Understanding the climate.
Understanding culture.
Understanding people.
And understanding the complex relationships that already exist before the architect arrives.
Only then can design become meaningful.
Because the most relevant architecture does not simply occupy a place.
It understands where it belongs — and transforms that understanding into space.

posts.title: Habitus: Projekte nga MA Studio & Partners
posts.excerpt: 22 vite arkitekturë, transformim dhe një filozofi që vazhdon të evoluojë
body:
Çfarë qëndron pas një projekti arkitektonik? Si evoluon një studio pas më shumë se dy dekadash eksperiencë? Dhe si takohet arkitektura me tregun imobiliar në momentin kur një hapësirë e projektuar shndërrohet në një shtëpi për dikë?
Në një episod të Habitus, programi i autorit Qazim Strazimiri, arkitektët Ervin Taçi dhe Klodiana Taçi sjellin historinë, filozofinë dhe projektet e MA Studio & Partners, ndërsa Pranvera Shkurta, konsulente imobiliare pranë RE/MAX Infinity, na çon në anën tjetër të banimit: procesin real të kërkimit dhe përzgjedhjes së një apartamenti.
Dy perspektiva të ndryshme, por të lidhura nga i njëjti element: hapësira ku jetojmë.
Ervin & Klodiana Taçi: 22 vite rrugëtim në arkitekturë
Historia e MA Studio & Partners nuk fillon dy vite më parë.
Pas identitetit të sotëm të studios qëndron një rrugëtim profesional më shumë se 20-vjeçar, i ndërtuar mbi eksperiencë, projekte, transformime dhe mbi të gjitha mbi një marrëdhënie të vazhdueshme me arkitekturën.
Për rreth dy dekada, ky rrugëtim u identifikua me DEA Studio, një brand i njohur në skenën shqiptare të projektimit.
Sot, kjo eksperiencë vazhdon përmes MA Studio & Partners.
Dy vitet e MA Studio & Partners përfaqësojnë kështu jo fillimin e një historie të re nga zero, por një kapitull të ri të një historie 22-vjeçare.
Në Habitus, Ervin dhe Klodiana Taçi flasin pikërisht për këtë evolucion: për mënyrën sesi eksperienca transformon këndvështrimin e arkitektit, për filozofinë që qëndron pas projekteve dhe për përgjegjësinë që arkitektura ka ndaj njerëzve, kontekstit dhe qytetit.
Nga DEA Studio te MA Studio & Partners
Transformimi nga DEA Studio në MA Studio & Partners shënon një evolucion të natyrshëm profesional.
Një studio arkitekture, njësoj si arkitektura që krijon, nuk mund të mbetet statike.
Ajo ndryshon me njerëzit, me eksperiencën, me teknologjinë, me mënyrën e të jetuarit dhe me sfidat e reja që sjell çdo projekt.
MA Studio & Partners ndërton mbi trashëgiminë profesionale të DEA Studio, duke e çuar atë drejt një strukture të re bashkëpunimi dhe një vizioni më të gjerë për arkitekturën dhe dizajnin.
Në qendër mbetet bindja se një projekt i mirë nuk është thjesht rezultat estetik.
Ai lind nga kuptimi i vendit, funksionit, materialit dhe, mbi të gjitha, i njeriut që do ta përjetojë hapësirën.
Projektet: nga ideja te hapësira e ndërtuar
Përmes projekteve të realizuara dhe atyre aktualisht në proces, episodi hap një dritare drejt mënyrës sesi funksionon një studio arkitekture.
Nga koncepti fillestar dhe skicat e para, te zhvillimi teknik, materiali, detaji dhe realizimi përfundimtar, çdo projekt është rezultat i një procesi kompleks vendimmarrjeje.
Habitus krijon pikërisht hapësirën për të parë përtej imazhit final.
Jo vetëm çfarë është projektuar, por edhe pse është projektuar në atë mënyrë.
Projektet e MA Studio & Partners bëhen kështu pikënisje për të diskutuar arkitekturën si proces: marrëdhënien me klientin, interpretimin e programit, kufizimet e kontekstit dhe mënyrën sesi një ide gradualisht merr formë fizike.
Kur arkitektura takohet me real estate
Por historia e një banese nuk përfundon kur arkitekti mbyll projektin.
Në shumë raste, aty fillon një proces tjetër: tregu imobiliar.
Në të njëjtin episod, Pranvera Shkurta, konsulente imobiliare pranë RE/MAX Infinity, sjell një eksperiencë konkrete nga puna e saj, duke shoqëruar një kliente që kërkon të blejë një apartament për prindërit.
Në pamje të parë është një transaksion imobiliar.
Në realitet, është një proces shumë më njerëzor.
Kur një apartament kërkohet për prindërit, kriteret ndryshojnë. Vendndodhja, aksesueshmëria, organizimi i hapësirave, drita natyrale, komoditeti, siguria dhe funksionaliteti marrin një rëndësi të veçantë.
Konsulenti imobiliar nuk kërkon më thjesht një pronë që përmbush një buxhet dhe një sipërfaqe të caktuar.
Duhet të kuptojë mënyrën sesi njerëzit do të jetojnë brenda saj.
Dhe pikërisht këtu real estate takohet përsëri me arkitekturën.
Një apartament nuk është vetëm metra katrorë
Një nga perspektivat interesante që sjell Habitus është mundësia për ta parë banesën nga dy anë.
Nga njëra anë është arkitekti, i cili mendon për proporcionin, funksionin, dritën, materialin dhe eksperiencën hapësinore.
Nga ana tjetër është konsulenti imobiliar, i cili duhet të kuptojë nevojat konkrete të personit që do ta blejë dhe jetojë atë hapësirë.
Në mes qëndron banesa.
Jo vetëm si aset financiar.
Jo vetëm si sipërfaqe e shprehur në metra katrorë.
Por si hapësirë jetese.
Sepse vlera reale e një apartamenti përcaktohet edhe nga mënyra sesi arkitektura e tij i përgjigjet jetës së përditshme.
Habitus: të kuptojmë hapësirat ku jetojmë
Me autor Qazim Strazimiri, Habitus sjell në vëmendje projektet arkitektonike të realizuara dhe në proces nga disa prej studiove më të mira në vend, duke krijuar një hapësirë ku publiku mund të njohë më nga afër procesin e dizajnit dhe projektimit të strukturave me karaktere dhe funksione të ndryshme.
Paralelisht, programi ndjek edhe proceset e transaksioneve imobiliare, me një fokus të veçantë te banesa dhe te vendimet që shoqërojnë blerjen e saj.
Kjo ndërthurje e bën Habitus një bisedë jo vetëm për profesionistët e arkitekturës apo të real estate, por për këdo që kërkon të kuptojë më mirë si projektohen, si zgjidhen dhe si jetohen hapësirat tona.
Episodi me MA Studio & Partners dhe RE/MAX Infinity e shpreh qartë këtë marrëdhënie.
Nga 22 vitet e eksperiencës së Ervin dhe Klodiana Taçit, nga historia e DEA Studio te kapitulli i ri MA Studio & Partners, nga projektet në tavolinën e arkitektit te kërkimi konkret për një apartament për dy prindër — në fund, të gjitha historitë bashkohen te i njëjti koncept:
Arkitektura fillon me hapësirën.
Por merr kuptim vetëm kur brenda saj fillon jeta.

posts.title: Open Studio: “Modelling Architecture” Exhibition Opens in Tirana
posts.excerpt: Drawings, models and process work from a decade of practice go on show at the studio. The exhibition runs all month, with guided walkthroughs each weekend.

posts.title: Adriatic Coastal Masterplan Shortlisted for the Mies Award
posts.excerpt: Our coastal masterplan framework was named to the shortlist for the EU Mies van der Rohe Award, recognised for balancing public access, ecology and resilient growth along the Adriatic.
